problem_shape: This family is about turning a language model from a talker into a worker. The real object is not just an answer in a chat box. It is a chain of actions: choosing a search tool, calling a ranker, reading a database schema, using memory from earlier sessions, asking another agent to review a plan, or deciding that a simple question should not spend much computing power. The input file shows this across shopping, search, machine-learning workflow construction, book finding, mobile control, software development, emotional support, policy simulation, content moderation, and privacy-literacy tools. The shared pressure is that real tasks sit outside the model. Useful facts live in documents, web pages, tools, databases, user histories, first-person video, or platform logs. A worker must decide what to fetch, what to ignore, when to ask another component, and when to stop. That makes the family a study of controlled action under uncertainty: the agent must map a vague human request onto a sequence of concrete, checkable steps without losing the user goal.
naive_failure: A smart beginner would first give the model a big instruction: understand the request, pick any useful tool, and explain the final answer. That can work for small demonstrations, but the input papers repeatedly show why it breaks in real settings. Tool documentation may not use the same words as the user, so a tool selector retrieves the wrong API. Long conversations and biological sequences overflow the useful working memory, so important facts vanish. Multi-agent systems can add noise instead of clarity, as the feedback-generation paper reports when a well-designed single prompt often beats agent splitting. Production shopping agents must meet accuracy, latency, reliability, and cost limits at the same time. Security papers show a sharper failure: poisoned tool context or malicious knowledge-base documents can make the agent spend extra money or take unsafe actions. The simple plan fails because action creates consequences, not just text.
mathematical_principle: The repeated mathematical idea is controlled search through a large menu of possible next moves. At each step, the agent has a goal, partial evidence, and many possible actions: rewrite the query, retrieve a tool, call a search system, consult memory, compress context, ask a specialist agent, roll back a suspicious state, or end the task. The math turns this into scoring and choice. Some papers train the chooser from reward: actions that lead to better tool use, stronger ranking, or fewer failed tasks receive more credit. Some arrange examples from easier to harder, so the model first learns clean choices before facing noisy and conflicting ones. Some route work by estimated difficulty, sending simple questions through cheaper paths and hard ones through deeper reasoning. Retrieval papers measure closeness between the user need and tool descriptions, documents, AppCards, schemas, or knowledge-graph facts. Security and evaluation papers measure deviation: does the current tool context, explanation, or user behavior look unlike a trusted path? The core tradeoff is exploration versus reliability, with cost, memory, and safety as hard operational limits in practice.
why_math_matters: The math matters because the world has structure that a handwritten rule list cannot cover. User requests are varied, but many reduce to the same hidden question: which small set of outside resources should be trusted for this step? Tool repositories are huge, yet tools with related documentation, inputs, and past success patterns should be nearer to each other than unrelated tools. Dialogue histories are long, yet only some past facts matter for the present emotional-support reply. Mobile apps and web shopping flows differ, yet an agent can reuse the pattern of finding intent, gathering evidence, comparing options, and acting. Reward-based learning fits because success is often visible after the sequence: the workflow runs, the item ranking helps, the Android task succeeds, the policy simulation changes a predicted outcome, or the answer is grounded in retrieved evidence. The structure is not perfect, so the papers add filters, staged training, debate, rollback, routing, and explicit memory to keep the choice process from becoming blind confidence.
paper_family: The tool-use papers are siblings because they all build gates between language and action. TOOL-CURE and Tool-Star focus on choosing and coordinating tools, using staged practice and feedback from success to reduce wrong calls. ToolBox-RL faces the same shape at repository scale: rewrite a user need, understand intent, and retrieve the right tool even when the words do not match the documentation. MCP servers for Pyserini and RankLLM expose search and ranking tools so an agent can ground answers in retrieval instead of guessing. The production shopping agent, Smart Book Seeker, and conversational search work apply the same gate to commerce and library discovery: turn a messy preference into retrieval, comparison, and action. PromptX, ES-MemEval, Frugal Agents, and the egocentric co-pilot treat memory and compressed context as tools that must be opened only when useful. CodeForge, COMA, GCAgent, and automated software-development agents split work across roles, but still face the same question: which voice or module should influence the next step? Security papers such as MCP remediation and cost attacks study what happens when the gate is deliberately misled before action.
what_changed: The 2026 version shown here moves from impressive single-agent demos toward operating conditions. Many papers are about production limits, not just task scores: Amazon-scale shopping requires latency, cost, and reliability; EcoThink routes easy questions to save energy; TCR compresses heavier reasoning into a smaller ranker for real-time recommendation; Frugal Agents reduce long-context expense. The family also becomes more defensive. Tool poisoning, retrieval cost attacks, noisy user behavior, and biased code reasoning are treated as central problems. Finally, agents are becoming situated: they work over phone apps, web shopping, smart glasses video, group chats, therapy stages, historical-character data, and relational databases rather than only clean text prompts.
limits: These papers assume that the agent can observe enough of the task to score its own progress or learn from past success. That may fail when the user goal is vague, private, changing, or only judged long after the action. Retrieval-based tool use assumes useful tools and documents can be found from descriptions; sparse metadata, poisoned entries, or missing evidence break that assumption. Multi-agent debate assumes separate roles add checks, but the feedback-generation result warns that splitting a task can lower consistency. Memory helps only if stored facts are true, current, and relevant. Simulations and benchmarks show controlled evidence, not proof that agents will behave safely under every deployment pressure, adversary, language, user literacy level, or cost constraint.
